title: The insidious, fascinating, and utterly infuriating reason that women’s health care is worse than men’s
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
The insidious, fascinating, and utterly infuriating reason that women’s health care is worse than men’s

How the medical system literally devalues women’s bodies.

Actual Article Body:
When news breaks, you need to understand what actually matters — and what to do about it. At Vox, our mission to help you make sense of the world has never been more vital. But we can’t do it on our own.

We rely on readers like you to fund our journalism. Will you support our work and become a Vox Member today?

How the medical system literally devalues women’s bodies.

In the moody alcoves of a lobby bar in Chicago in 2021 over French 75s, Dr. Louise King, a gynecologic surgeon, and Katie L. Watson, a bioethics professor, found themselves in conversation about a topic that had long frustrated them both: Female surgeons are consistently underpaid compared to male surgeons, even after accounting for specialty, rank, age, and other factors.

What troubled them even more was how the pay gap compounded in King’s own field. Surgeons who perform procedures that are specifically for women, like gynecological surgeries, are paid less for their services than surgeons who perform comparable surgeries for the male anatomy. Gynecologic surgeons are also predominantly women. Over the course of the conversation, Watson termed this situation “double discrimination,” a phrase that captures the overlapping dilemma of lower pay for surgeries in a specialty that is overwhelmingly female and also serves a primarily female patient population.

That term, which has since entered the medical literature, stuck because the problem it describes has been well documented for decades. In 1997, a group of gynecologic surgeons published a paper in the journal Gynecologic Oncology with a title that gets straight to it — “Is Adam worth more than Eve?” Dr. Barbara A. Goff, now chair of Obstetrics and Gynecology at University of Washington Medicine, and colleagues found that doctors are paid around 44 percent more for performing male-specific procedures than analogous female-specific ones.

In the three decades since, the problem hasn’t been fixed. To the contrary, it has been effectively institutionalized, built into the systems and codes that determine how surgeons bill for procedures of all kinds. Today, gynecologic or female-specific procedures are in large parts still reimbursed at lower rates than male-specific procedures even when they take similar time and skill.

Those disparities have consequences that extend beyond the compensation of individual doctors. When gynecological procedures don’t bring in as much money to hospitals, those same hospitals are disincentivised to offer women’s health services. That can lead to worse care for women and, crucially, fewer training opportunities for the surgeons who do that work.

But this historically persistent inequality is not a foregone conclusion.

How healthcare services are billed changes all the time as procedures get reevaluated, new ones get added, and medical societies and experts push for revisions. In fact, one of the biggest changes in how maternity care is billed and reimbursed is set to take effect early next year, splitting up services for prenatal care, delivery, postpartum care, and more. While this is a long-overdue fix for obstetrics, gynecologic surgery — which covers most of a woman’s life outside of childbearing years — continues to be left out of the conversation.

And although real change will require concerted efforts, King and Watson — and other advocates who have spent years documenting this disparity — have a fairly clear sense of how to start fixing it.

The work of deciding how much a medical procedure is worth starts well above the head of any given doctor, medical practice, or hospital. In the United States, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, a federal agency that administers healthcare and health insurance policies, sets rates for different procedures based on a metric called relative value units (RVUs).
